{"publish":true,"title":"Recurrent Neural Networks","tags":["CS2109S","artificial_intelligence","neural_networks"],"cssclasses":""}
---

 # Motivation

RNNs are used for **sequential data**, where:


> [!definition] Sequential data
> Refers to data where the order of elements matters, and each element depends on its position in the sequence.

Examples of data where this matters are:
- text data (sentences)
- audio/video data

# One-Hot Encoding

For each word, create a vector with length equal to the **vocabulary size**, Each word is then assigned a unique index, and its corresponding vector is all zeros except for a `1` in the position of that index.

For example: given the sentence `we saw this saw`, the one-hot encoded vector is something like:

```
[
	# words in order
	[1, 0, 0, 0], # we
	[0, 1, 0, 1], # saw
	[0, 0, 1, 0]  # this
]
```

> [!question] Why does a simple neural network not work?

For example, when predicting word classes in a sentence, due to grammatical and syntax rules, the same word can change meaning/class based on the context. Thus, a recurrent neural network is needed.

Thus, at every time step $t$, the hidden state is represented as:

$$
h^{t}= \begin{bmatrix}
h_{1}^{t} \\ h_{2}^{t}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

and that hidden state is updated constantly with:

$$
h^{t} = \bbox[lavender, 5px]{\color{black} g^{[h]}(\bbox[lime, 5px]{\color{black} W^{[xh]]}})^{T}x^{t}+(\bbox[pink, 5px]{\color{black} W^{[hh]}})^{T}h^{t-1}} 
$$

and the value of the prediction $y^{t}$ is:

$$
\hat{y}^{t}= \bbox[lavender, 5px]{\color{black} g^{[y]}((\bbox[cyan, 5px]{\color{black} W^{[hy]}})^{T}h^{t})}
$$

> [!pros] Captures context information

> [!cons] Prediction at $t$ requires all $1.. t-1$ to be complete, which is not parallelism-friendly.

# Self Attention Layer

A self-attention layer captures contextual information from other parts of the input sequence.

The query and key weights are stored in the weights $w_{q}, w_{k}$.

Thus, for each feature $x^{[i]}$, the query can be calculated:

$$
q^{i}= W^{q}x^{[i]}
$$

Then the key for another feature $x^{[j]}$ can be calculated:

$$
k^{j} = W^{k}x^{[j]}
$$

The attention score $\alpha_{ij}$ refers to how much context the feature $x^{[j]}$ provides to the feature $x^{[i]}$. 

$$
\alpha_{ij} = k^{j} \cdot q^{i} = (k^{j})^{T} q^{i}
$$

A simplified expansion of the self-attention layer over two features can be seen:

**Step 1**: Linear projection

We can use matrix multiplication to generate the $Q, K, V$ matrix.

For example:

$$
Q = \begin{bmatrix} 
q^{1} & .. & q^{n}
\end{bmatrix} = W^{q}\begin{bmatrix} 
x^{1} & .. & x^{n}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute attention scores

Similarly with the same logic, since the attention score $\alpha_{ij}$ is calculated as $\bbox[lime, 5px]{\color{black} (k^{j})^{T}}\bbox[lavender, 5px]{\color{black} q^{i}}$, we can use the matrix multiplication:

$$
\bbox[pink, 5px]{\color{black} A = \bbox[lime, 5px]{\color{black} K^{T}} \bbox[lavender, 5px]{\color{black} Q}}
$$

The attention matrix will look something like this:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\alpha_{11} & \alpha_{21} & ... & \alpha_{k1} \\
\alpha_{12} & \alpha_{22} & ... & \alpha_{k2} \\ 
... & ... & ...  & ... \\
\alpha_{1j} & \alpha_{2j} & ... & \alpha_{kj} \\ 
\end{bmatrix}
$$

**Step 3:** Apply softmax, column-wise into the attention matrix

**Step 4:** Get weighted sum

We can get a singular output $h^{i}$ by:

$$
h^{i} = V A^{[i]}
$$

Use matrix multiplication on the $V$ and softmaxed $A'$ attention score matrix to get all the outputs.

$$
H = VA
$$

# Positional Encoding

Add positional information to differentiate.

> [!definition] Positional encoding
> Explicitly injects positional information into original input features.


$$
x^{'i} = x^{i} + PE^{i}
$$

where $PE^{i}$ refers to the positional encoding vector.

The positional encoding vector is generated using $\sin$ and $\cos$ functions:

$$
PE(i, 2k) = \sin(\frac{i}{10000^{\frac{2k}{d}}}), PE(i, 2k+1) = \cos(\frac{i}{10000^{\frac{2k}{d}}}), 0 \leq k \leq \frac{d}{2}-1
$$
